patient.chief_complaint: Drooping eyelids, double vision, and difficulty chewing
patient.history_present_illness: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, COPD, and prostate cancer on active surveillance presented for evaluation of progressive bilateral ptosis, double vision, and difficulty chewing over 3 months. His wife first noticed his eyelids drooping approximately 3 months ago, initially intermittent and worse in the afternoons. He then developed horizontal diplopia when looking to the left, which was intermittent and positional. He began having difficulty chewing tough foods — he would tire out halfway through a meal and would need to rest his jaw. He has lost approximately 4 pounds over the past 2 months because he avoids foods that require prolonged chewing. He denies dysphagia with liquids but acknowledges occasional difficulty with large solid boluses. His voice has become softer and more nasal sounding after talking for more than 5 minutes, which his wife has noticed. He has no history of neck or back pain, no extremity weakness at rest, no falls, no bowel or bladder dysfunction. He was initially referred to ophthalmology who noted no structural eyelid pathology and no proptosis. He was then seen by his primary care physician who ordered brain MRI, which was reportedly normal. He was subsequently referred to the neurology clinic where examination revealed clear fatigability. His COPD is well-controlled on tiotropium with moderate exercise tolerance. The pulmonologist was concerned about overlapping respiratory muscle weakness potentially contributing to his reduced exercise capacity. He has not had any recent infections or antibiotic treatments. He denies weight loss beyond the 4 pounds from reduced food intake.

output.proposed: Prednisone for immunosuppression in MG in patient with Type 2 DM on metformin (HbA1c 7.8%)
interactions: Prednisone + metformin: corticosteroids antagonize insulin secretion and cause hyperglycemia; metformin will be insufficient to control steroid-induced hyperglycemia

contraindications: High-dose steroids as sole initial MG therapy without glucose monitoring plan is dangerous in T2DM
Consider initiating insulin for glycemic control during steroid therapy

Intensify glucose monitoring — check BG before meals and at bedtime
Consider endocrinology consultation for steroid-diabetes management

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, with thymoma; complicated by COPD, type 2 diabetes, and low-risk prostate cancer

differential.key_features: Smoking history and prostate cancer raise paraneoplastic concern; however, baseline CMAP normal here, high-rate RNS does not show >100% facilitation, anti-VGCC negative expected.
COPD can cause dyspnea but does not produce fatigable ptosis, diplopia, or RNS decrement.
Cervical spine disease can cause weakness but not fatigable ptosis/diplopia or NMJ-pattern RNS.
Diabetic microvascular cranial neuropathy is monocular and acute, not bilateral and fluctuating.
No fixed lateralized deficit, MRI without acute lesion, fluctuating pattern excludes stroke.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: CT chest with contrast — thymoma identified (anterior mediastinal mass 2.2 x 1.8 cm)
Refer to thoracic surgery for thymectomy after MG optimization
Coordinate steroid plan with diabetes team given HbA1c 7.8% — high-dose prednisone will require insulin adjustment
Pre-treatment respiratory function (FVC, MIP/MEP) given COPD baseline (GOLD Stage 2)
Avoid fluoroquinolones for any infection — bronchitis exacerbation common in COPD
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT prescribe respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) for COPD exacerbation in this patient — substitute with macrolide or beta-lactam.
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Anti-titin or anti-RyR antibodies in an MG patient strongly predict thymoma — CT chest is mandatory and surgical referral is non-negotiable.
Late-onset MG (>50y) commonly presents with thymoma — CT chest mandatory; this patient's anti-titin antibody further supports thymoma association.
COPD + diabetes complicate steroid initiation: plan glucose management and rehabilitation up front.

red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral upper-lobe emphysematous changes (chronic COPD) on CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute dyspnea solely to COPD and miss MG/thymoma diagnosis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: COPD changes are chronic and unrelated; the actionable finding is the anterior mediastinal mass — thymoma; fatigable bulbar/ocular weakness is the MG signature.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on diabetes-related cranial neuropathy as the cause of ptosis/diplopia.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetic cranial neuropathy is acute, painful, and monocular; this is fluctuating, bilateral, fatigable — classic MG.
